en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Śīladhara of Xisi Monastery in Weiguo, Jingzhao Prefecture.
From here below is the second section, which further elucidates the essential characteristics of the causal conditions upon which [the teaching] relies. This section contains two parts:
first, a brief clarification of the profound nature of dependent origination; second, from the words "That which is called the nature of mind" onwards, a detailed exposition.
Regarding the meaning of the distinctions within dependent origination,
there are two parts in the first section;
first, the heading praises its profundity.
Regarding the subsequent section that explains the reason for its profundity:
as for the phrase "consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance" at the beginning, it refers to consciousness produced by the habitual influence of ignorance.

This summarizes what was explained above: that based on fundamental ignorance, those tranquil minds give rise to the consciousnesses of karma and so forth. Below is the formal praise of its profound depth;
therein, first, it is shown that this is beyond the reach of ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle.
Next, this is known partially by Bodhisattvas;
ultimately, it is only the Buddha who fully comprehends it.

It is not something that ordinary beings can know, nor is it what the wisdom of the two vehicles can awaken to, because those of the two vehicles only awaken to the four abodes [of afflictions] but do not comprehend ignorance (*avidyā*).
This consciousness arising from ignorance is not its object.

That is to say, from the initial arousal of the mind through right faith, when a bodhisattva observes and realizes the dharmakāya, they attain a partial knowledge; yet even up to the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva, they cannot know it exhaustively—it is only the Buddha who fully comprehends it. Regarding the phrase "from the initial arousal of the mind through right faith," etc.: [this refers to the stages beginning with the first resolve].
At the very beginning of the ten stages of faith, when first generating the aspiration for enlightenment,
one contemplates the essence of the causal and resultant aspects of the self-nature dependent origination of the fundamental consciousness,
thereby attaining right faith.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states regarding that fundamental consciousness:
"When a bodhisattva first gives rise to [the aspiration for awakening], they should first contemplate all phenomena according to their true causes and conditions.
This is what that refers to.
Within the stage of the three types of worthies, one engages in conceptual observation through mental discourse;
therefore, it is called "contemplation. On the stages of the bodhisattva grounds, although this is realized through direct perception, it is not yet exhaustive.
Therefore, it is said that they possess only a partial [realization]. This is because they perceive only the characteristic of abiding and do not perceive the characteristic of arising,
whereas the Tathāgata fully understands all four characteristics.
This is the attainment of the ultimate source. Why is this so? The following section explains the reason for its profundity.
Why is this so? First, the underlying intent is questioned as follows:
the wondrous principle of dependent origination permeates both the ordinary and the sagely.
Why is it said that "seeing" exists only in those who have attained the fruit? The answer consists of three parts:

first, that although there is purity, there is also defilement; second, that although there is a defiled mind, [the nature] is fundamentally pure; third, that although there is defilement, it is eternally pure.
Third, for this reason, the conclusion below establishes that it is unfathomable;
therefore, only a Buddha knows it.
Within the preceding section, there are three phrases.

This mind has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning, yet through ignorance it becomes defiled by that ignorance; thus there is a "defiled mind. This initial essence of dependent origination is the cause.
Next, the cause for the arising of dependent origination is presented; this is "conditionality.
Finally, the characteristic of dependent origination is revealed;
this is "being defiled while remaining undefiled."

Although there is a defiled mind, it is eternally constant and unchanging; therefore, this meaning can be known only by a Buddha. This passage below explains the profound meaning of dependent origination:
that although it is defiled, it is not defiled.
The Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra states:
"The intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend;
that mind is defiled by afflictions."
It is likewise difficult to comprehend;
it concludes by stating that only a Buddha can know it.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also speaks in this same way.
Therefore, that sutra says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is by nature pure;
it is defiled and impure only by adventitious afflictions."
...and so on, as explained at length.
The conclusion below states:
"I now [entrust this] to you and to all the bodhisattvas who possess profound wisdom."
It is capable of discerning [this]. ○ Second, regarding the phrase "so-called," below is the extensive manifestation of the distinct characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This section contains two parts.
First, the manifestation of the essential nature and characteristics of the aforementioned dependent origination.
Regarding the second point, "not understanding the meaning of a single dharma," the following provides a further detailed analysis.
This section consists of three parts.
The first, "the nature of the mind," explains the meaning of immutability mentioned above.
Because the nature of the mind is eternally free from thought, it is called immutable; although its entire substance moves, it is fundamentally quiescent.
Therefore, it is said: "Always without thought.

This reveals the essence of the causal origination of conditions mentioned above. Second, "Because of not attaining [realization]... and so forth, reveals the reason for the causal origination of ignorance mentioned above.

Because one does not attain realization of the single dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*), thoughts arise suddenly in a manner dissociated from the mind; this is termed ignorance (*avidyā*). This also explains the reason why ignorance arises, as mentioned above.
Because one does not understand the single meaning of the equality of *tathatā*,
the mind, though non-associated [with mental factors], suddenly experiences a movement of thought;
this is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
This reveals that fundamental ignorance is extremely subtle, lacking any differentiation between subject and object or between the primary mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*);
because it is a delusion of the mind itself, it is called "non-associated.
It does not mean that it is associated with the primary mind and its mental factors in the same way they are mutually associated.
Only this ignorance is the source of all defiled phenomena;
it is most extremely subtle,
and there is no other defiled phenomenon capable of serving as its basis.
Therefore, it is said that thoughts arise suddenly.
As the *Yingluo benye jing* states:
"Prior to the four stages of abiding (catur-vihāra-bhūmi), no further dharmas can arise."
This is called the "ground of beginningless ignorance" (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
This clarifies that prior to ignorance there is no other distinct dharma that serves as the fundamental basis for its initial accumulation;
therefore, it is said to be "beginningless."
This refers precisely to the meaning of "sudden" (*akasmāt*) in this treatise.
This is explained as being "without precedent" (*apūrva*) from the perspective of the mutual dependence of the coarse and the subtle;
thus it is also called "sudden."
It is not said that it occurs "suddenly" by way of disregarding time and season, because its arising has no beginning.
Regarding the phrase "the defiled mind," this is the third section below, which clarifies the characteristics of dependent origination;
it refers to the statement concerning the existence of a defiled mind.
Within this, there are three parts:
the heading, the inquiry, and the detailed explanation.
Within the detailed explanation:
The six defilements consist of the higher consciousness and the five types of mental consciousness; however,
because the preceding section clarifies the meaning of the sequential order of arising based on causes and conditions,
they are explained here from the subtle to the coarse.
Now, wishing to distinguish and explain the sequence of their abandonment,
they are discussed from the coarse to the subtle;
within each of the six categories, there are two.
First, the obstacles; later, their remedies.
Regarding the defiled mind, there are six kinds. What are these six? First is the defilement associated with grasping (*saṃprayukta-kleśa*).
As for this first defilement associated with grasping, it consists of the grasping at signs (*nimitta-grāha*) and the calculating of names (*nāma-vikalpa*) among the six coarse [defilements].
This also signifies that which is increased by the afflictions of craving and attachment within the higher mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is also the characteristic of coarse conceptualization and clinging among the four aforementioned characteristics.
It refers merely to the external grasping of the coarse mind.
It is called "defiled" because it is stained by association with sense objects, thereby defiling pure conduct.

It is so called because it is far removed from the liberation of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and the stage associated with faith (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*). As for the two vehicles, when they reach the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*), they have ultimately abandoned the afflictions of both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Regarding those who are associated with faith:
from the stage of the ten understandings onward,
they have perfected the faculty of faith and are free from any regression or loss.
This is called "correspondence with faith. Therefore,
in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages),
those prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path] are collectively termed "bodhisattvas of the stage of practice through faith" (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*).
The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra* also states this in the same way.

Because these bodhisattvas have realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the afflictions of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-kleśa*) cannot manifest; therefore, it is said that they are "far removed."
This does not refer to the latent dispositions (anuśaya), because [bodhisattvas] intentionally retain these afflictions.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
If one does not sever the superior mind,
then one is no different from an ordinary person;
if one does not retain the seeds, [then one is liberated].
In that case, they would not differ from the two vehicles.
Furthermore, there are two intentions for retaining afflictions: for one’s own sake and for the sake of others.
This is explained according to the Final Teaching (Ultimate Vehicle).
If one refers to the Initial Teaching (śāstra),
it is only from the first bhūmi upward that the retention of afflictions is taught,
as stated in other treatises.
Now, this bodhisattva not only severs the personhood-clinging of the four abodes, but also partially severs the ground-abode of ignorance;
as the latter part of this treatise states: "Those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm..."
Because one observes and trains in abandonment from the stage of association with faith (*śraddhā-pratipannaka-bhūmi*),
[the author] now merely intends to reveal the coarse grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*) and does not discuss those [other views].

Second, because one gradually abandons the defilement associated with non-interruption through the practice of skillful means on the stage of faith-correspondence, attaining the ultimate detachment of the pure mind-ground. Regarding "the second, the association with non-interruption": [it refers to] the defilement associated with non-interruption.
Among the five aspects of mental content, it is called "continuous consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).
Among the six coarse aspects, it is called the "aspect of continuity.
It refers simply to the uninterrupted arising of the continuous production of the grasping at dharmas (*dharma-grāha*).
"Uninterrupted" is a synonym for "continuity.

From the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) onward, one cultivates the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) through the skillful means of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*),
until reaching the first bhūmi, where one realizes the three natures of non-being and the all-pervading suchness (*tathatā*).
Because the conceptualization of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*) cannot manifest, it is said that it is "ultimately abandoned" at the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*).

Third, regarding the defilement associated with the conceptualizing wisdom (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*): it is gradually abandoned from the Stage of Perfect Precepts (*suviśuddha-śīla-bhūmi*) until it is ultimately abandoned at the Stage of Skillful Means for the Signless (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*). Thus, it is "associated with the conceptualizing wisdom."
This is the wisdom-consciousness among the five mental states;
it is the aspect of wisdom among the six coarse factors.
It is able to discern the defiled and pure aspects of all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "wisdom.
This refers to the afflictions of attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha-kleśa) from the seventh stage downward.
Because there are differences between entering and emerging from meditative absorption, there is subtle discrimination regarding the objects of perception;
however, this is progressively eliminated stage by stage.
Therefore, it is said that one gradually departs [from them].
From the eighth stage onward,
there is no longer any external objective realm apart from meditative observation.
Therefore, these delusions are exhausted at the seventh stage.
Thus it is said that they are ultimately abandoned in the "Stage of Skillful Means of Signlessness.
This is because the threefold aggregate of precepts is fully perfected in the second stage.
It is called the stage of possessing the precepts because,
in the seven stages, there is the functional application of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) within the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*).
It is called the stage of the skillful means of signlessness.
Because from the eighth stage onward, there is no effort regarding signlessness or skillful means.

Fourth, the defilement of non-conformity with manifested forms can be abandoned through mastery over the self-nature of form. Regarding "non-conformity with manifested forms": [it refers to the following].
The manifest consciousness within the aforementioned five mental states is the aspect of objective realms within the aforementioned three subtle states;
it is like a clear mirror manifesting forms and images.
This refers to the movement of fundamental ignorance which causes the manifest objects to appear.
Because one attains mastery over the three worlds in the eighth stage,
the nature of form conforms to the mind without any obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that the stage of mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśitā*) is able to transcend [form].
This is because in the stage where form lacks mastery, the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*) has not yet ceased;
thus, within this stage, one eliminates those appearances.
Fifth, because one is able to see that the defilements dissociated from mind can be abandoned by means of the mastery over the mind itself. Regarding "the five who are able to see the mind":
this refers to the evolving consciousnesses among the five types of mental activity (*manas*).
Among the three subtleties, the characteristic of being able to see arises because fundamental ignorance moves [the mind] so that it can see.
As stated in the preceding text:
Because the capacity for seeing is established based on the moving mind,
one thoroughly understands the ten kinds of dense forests of sentient beings' mental activities in the ninth stage; therefore,
it is called "mastery over the mind."
He attains mastery over the minds of others.
Furthermore, having himself attained the forty kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*),
any obstructed cognitive objects can never arise again.
Therefore, it is said that the stage of mastery over the mind (*cittavaśitā*) is able to bring about detachment.

Sixth, because the bodhisattva, having exhausted the stages (*bhūmi*), enters the stage of the Tathāgata and is thus able to detach from the six root karmas that are inconsistent with [enlightenment]. Regarding the six root karmas:
The karmic consciousness among the five mental states is the phase of karmic activity among the three subtle states;
because of the power of ignorance, one fails to realize that the mind moves.

Regarding the phrase "the bodhisattva stage is exhausted," this refers to the fact that within the Vajropama-samādhi at the final moment of the tenth stage, and within the stainless stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*),
all subtle habitual tendencies and mental conceptions are completely extinguished.
The preceding text states:
"When one attains the vision of the nature of the mind,
the mind is then eternally abiding."
Therefore, it is said that one is "able to leave [it behind]. Second, within the further detailed examination, there are three parts.
First, distinguishing the aforementioned ignorance (*avidyā*) by examining it in terms of its antidotes and its abandonment.
Second, it explains the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*) and non-association (*asaṃprayoga*).
Third, it cites the defiled mind and ignorance from above,
establishing the meaning of the two types of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*) in relation to their objects.
The preceding section provides the headings and explanations.

Regarding those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*): from the stage of faith-correspondence (*śraddhā-pratipatti-bhūmi*), they observe, train, and sever [defilements] to enter the pure mind-ground (*vimala-citta-bhūmi*), where they attain detachment according to their respective degrees, up to the stage of the Tathāgata, where they are able to achieve ultimate detachment. This is the explanation within the commentary.
The initial coarse [afflictions] are abandoned upon reaching the first stage (bhūmi),
while the subsequent subtle ones are exhausted only upon reaching the Buddha-stage;
this refers precisely to the ground of ignorance (avidyā-āśraya) which serves as the basis for the aforementioned defiled mind.
Because that which can defile True Suchness (tathatā) constitutes a defiled mind;
as for what was stated above regarding the "destruction of the synthetic consciousness" (saṃghāta-vijñāna),
it refers to the extinction of ignorance (avidyā).
Regarding the cessation of the continuous mind:
because it severs the defiled mind,
although it is said that ignorance and the defiled mind have a temporal sequence, [they are in fact simultaneous].
However, their cultivation and cessation occur simultaneously.

Regarding the meaning of "association" (*saṃprayoga*), it refers to the fact that although the mind, mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), and phenomena have different bases and differ in terms of being defiled or pure, they are similar in their characteristics of cognition and their commonality of object. Second, the explanation of association and non-association: *Note: The provided text contains a partial definition of association followed by the heading for the second section on association and non-association.*
Among the six defilements, the first three are associated minds (*saṃprayukta-citta*).
Regarding "association," there are two explanations.
The first is explained in terms of the primary mind (*rāja*).
Because these three are all coarse states of mind,
it is said that "mind" and "mental factors" are distinct; here,
"mind" refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
"Mindfulness of dharmas" refers to mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Because the number of these factors differs from that of the [five] aggregates,
they are said to be "distinct."
In the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*,
these are termed "mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).
Regarding their distinction based on defilement and purity:

This is the object of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Regarding "knowing that the characteristics of the object and the characteristics of the cognition are identical": if the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) knows defilement, [it is because it perceives the identity between the characteristics of the object and the characteristics of the cognition].
The mental factors are also the same.
When the mind-king takes pure objects as its conditions,
the mental factors are likewise the same.
The identity of the characteristic of the knower is the identity of the knower;
the identity of the characteristic of the object is the identity of the object.
These two are explained in terms of the correspondence between mind and its objects.
Because these three types arise based on objects,
they are subsumed within the six aspects that arise based on objects mentioned in the preceding section.
The subsequent section states:
Because the objective sphere ceases, the associated mind ceases.
As for the statement that "mind and mental objects are distinct," "mind" refers to the cognizing mind.
"Dharma" refers to the object of cognition, the dharma-āyatana.
"Difference" means that the mind and its objects are not identical.
Regarding the phrase "based on defilement and purity, up to being identical": [it means that they are based on these states until they become one].
This means that one forms a defiled understanding toward defiled objects and a pure understanding toward pure objects; therefore,
it is said they are "the same."

The meaning of "non-associated" (*viprayukta*) refers to the fact that the mind itself is not awakened to the fact that it is eternally without distinction and does not possess the characteristics of a separate knower or of an object of cognition. Thus, the latter three [ignorances] and ignorance itself are all termed "non-associated."
This also has two explanations.
In the first explanation, which is based on the number of kings, it says:
"That is, the mind's lack of awakening is eternally without distinction."
This reveals that the essence of the mind is characterized by both movement and stillness within fundamental ignorance;
this very moving mind is the mark of non-awakening, and there is no further distinction between it and the sovereign consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Therefore, it is said that the non-awakening of the mind itself is always without distinction;

this reverses the previous notion that the mind and its objects are distinct. This is not the same as the case where the characteristic of knowing and the characteristic of the object-conditioned are different.
Since there is no distinction in terms of being a king or not,
how could there be such things as "knowing together" or "having the same cognitive object"?
The opposite of what was previously stated can be seen here.
These three kinds [of characteristics] arise based on non-awakening;
because they are not distinct from non-awakening, they are said to be "identical" (*jì*).
The preceding text states: "Based on non-awakening, the three characteristics arise."
Regarding "not awakening and not relinquishing":
this refers to the mind itself not awakening, and thus it is said to be "not relinquished.
It does not mean that they are associated [with each other] and therefore not separated.
The subsequent passage also states:
"Because ignorance ceases, the dissociated mind ceases.
This second point is also explained in terms of the relationship between the mind and its objects.
Regarding the statement "the mind itself is unaware," etc.,
it means that this ignorance is identical to this defiled mind and has no separate substance;
it does not refer to its association with external objects.
This very state of non-awakening exists solely within the fundamental mind; therefore,
it is said that "it is identical to the mind," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "different from the cognitions of characteristics and so forth," this distinguishes it from the previously mentioned associated [mental factors].
Since this non-associated mind is the ālayavijñāna, [it is distinct from those].
Within this, there is no distinction regarding the number of kings,
nor the meaning of non-correspondence with external objects, nor the meaning of being with or without discernment (*sa-vikalpa*/*nir-vikalpa*), and so forth.
Furthermore, this contradicts various treatises.
A reconciliation [of these points] is as explained in the separate record. Regarding the explanation of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), first the formal proposition is established.
The subsequent re-explanation consists of two parts: first, the obstacle of afflictions;
second, the obstacle to knowledge.

Furthermore, the meaning of "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-citta*) is termed the "obstruction of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of *tathatā*. Regarding the mention of "defiled mind" in the preceding section, it refers to the six types of defiled minds.
That which can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) reveals its meaning as an impediment; namely,
the wisdom that accords with reality, which is the sublime insight (*prajñā*) that illuminates quiescence.
This is called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*),
which is precisely what was described above as the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*).
The defiled mind, being agitated and discursive, opposes this state of tranquility.
Therefore, the defiled mind is termed the "obstruction of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
because it is agitated and disturbed by afflictions.
For now, this is explained according to the gate of mutual dependence between the root and its branches.
The defiled mind that arises is the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the ignorance (*avidyā*) that can give rise to that defiled mind is the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is not defined in terms of the two attachments to persons and phenomena.
This clarifies the two types of obstruction.
Regarding the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is termed an "obstruction to wisdom" because it can hinder the wisdom of spontaneous worldly activity.
What is called ignorance here is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
That which is able to obstruct mundane knowledge of activity (*karmajñāna*) reveals its meaning as an impediment; that is,
the subsequently attained knowledge of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatājñāna*).
This refers to the aforementioned inconceivable activity and function;
because ignorance is deluded and darkened, it lacks discrimination and thus opposes this function of wisdom.
It is called "obstruction to knowledge" (jñeyāvaraṇa), named after that which it obstructs.
What is the meaning of this? [This is explained] in the "Re-explanation" section.
The initial question states:
"Since this ignorance causes the essence of the mind to move and become a defiled mind through stillness and motion,
then ignorance must be subtle."
It should obstruct the wisdom of principle;
the defiled mind is coarse and should obstruct the wisdom of valid cognition.

Because, by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to perceive and manifest objects through false grasping, which contradicts the nature of equality. In the response, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is first explained.
Regarding the statement, "because, by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to perceive and manifest":
The latter three are the subtle defilements.
"Falsely grasping at objects" comprehensively subsumes the first three types of defiled mind.
Because they arise based on the same object,
that which contradicts the nature of equality explains the meaning of "obstruction."
Because this defiled mind differentiates between subject and object,
it opposes the fundamental wisdom in which subject and object are equal;
thus, it obstructs the realization of principle and wisdom.

Because all phenomena are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising, and because ignorance consists of non-awakening that falsely opposes the nature of phenomena, one is unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all worldly objects. This concludes the explanation of the obstruction to wisdom.
To say that all phenomena are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising refers to the nature of reality (dharmatā) as it is deluded by ignorance.
To say that ignorance fails to awaken and thus falsely opposes the nature of reality means:
This clearly reveals ignorance,
which contradicts the aforementioned dharmatā,
because it fails to comprehend the quiescence of phenomena as they truly are.
It is because false notions of arising and ceasing contradict the true nature of phenomena (dharma) that one cannot attain even the various forms of knowledge.
Because one is internally deluded regarding ultimate truth and perceives external objects through consciousness,
one is unable to accord with various cognitions regarding the sphere of conventional reality (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
This correctly explains the meaning of the wisdom that knows things as they are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) regarding obstacles.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing. Below this is the third part, which clarifies the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
herein there are three sections.
First, the number is stated and questions are raised; second, the names are listed to briefly reveal [the categories]; third, their characteristics are explained in detail.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of differentiated characteristics of arising and ceasing. What are the two? First, the coarse, which is associated with the mind; second, the subtle, which is dissociated from the mind. Regarding the former, it is said that the "coarse" is associated with the mind.
Among the six defilements, the first three are associated with the mind;
their characteristics are coarse and manifest,
and thus they are described in the sūtras as arising and ceasing.
Regarding those that are subtle and dissociated from the mind:
the latter three defilements are dissociated from the mind,
because they lack the coarse and manifest characteristics of mind and mental factors.
Its substance is subtle and flows constantly without interruption;
the sūtras describe this as the "flowing and ceasing" (pravṛtti-nirodha) of birth and death.
This is based on the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The tenth fascicle states:
"Consciousness has two kinds of cessation:
first, the cessation of characteristics."
Second, the cessation of the continuum;
birth and abiding are also like this.
These are the terms extracted from the Sūtra.
Since their distinct characteristics were not previously revealed, the Master of the Treatise now elucidates the two types— the coarse and the subtle—
of the mind’s marks of arising and ceasing, by way of the principles of association (*saṃprayoga*) and non-association (*asaṃprayoga*). This explanation consists of two parts.
First, it is elucidated by way of correlating [the stages] with persons;
subsequently, the basis for the characteristics is analyzed.
Regarding the first, it correlates [the stages] with persons across three positions.
Furthermore, among the coarse [levels], that which is the coarsest is the realm of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). The first three types of defiled minds are all termed "coarse";
among these, the first—the defilement associated with grasping—is even more coarse than the others.
This is said to be the coarsest among the coarse.
The stage of the three types of worthies is called the "inner ordinary person" (*prthagjana*).
Because they are able to perceive this defilement, it is termed the "sphere of the ordinary person."
The subtle within the coarse and the coarse within the subtle are the spheres of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, among the three preceding types of coarseness, the latter two refer to the defilement associated with non-interruption and the defilement associated with discriminative cognition.
This is slightly more subtle within the coarse mind;
hence it is called "the subtle within the coarse.
As for "the coarse within the subtle":
The latter three defiled minds are all termed "subtle.
Among them, the first two refer to those that are capable of seeing and manifesting;
they are termed subtle because they are equally dissociated from thought.
Because it follows after the fundamental karmic consciousness (*mūla-karma-vijñāna*) in form, it is further described as "coarse.
This is the object of knowledge within the stages of the Bodhisattvas from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) downwards.
That which is the subtlest among the subtle is the realm of the Buddhas. As for "the subtlest among the subtle":
This refers to the defilement that is not associated with the fundamental karmas;
because its subject and object have not yet been differentiated and its mode of activity is extremely subtle.
Only the Buddha can know this. From here below, the second section clarifies the meaning of the basis (*āśraya*), which has two parts:
first, a direct exposition of the conditions for arising;
second, a reverse discussion on the principle of cessation.
The preceding section also has two parts:

second, it reveals the specific causes.

These two types of arising and ceasing depend upon the permeation of ignorance; that which is called "depending on causes" has the meaning of non-awakening, while "depending on conditions" has the meaning of falsely constructing objective realms. Generally speaking, [this is so].
Both the coarse and subtle consciousnesses arise based on the ground of non-ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).
This is because the fundamental non-ignorance moves and gives rise to the three subtle states,
and based upon these three subtle states, the coarse mind subsequently arises.
Because ignorance serves as the pervasive root,
it is said that [the storehouse consciousness] exists through the perfuming of ignorance.
To speak of it specifically:
Based on the cause of ignorance, the three subtle non-associated minds arise;
based on the condition of objective realms, the three coarse associated minds arise.
Therefore, it is said: "Based on the cause, up to the point where one falsely constructs objective realms."
The text here is brief;
if explained in full,
each has two causes.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"O Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*)."
The grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization constitute the causes of the *vikaḷpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena).
The commentary explains:
"Inconceivable perfuming" refers to the fact that ignorance is able to perfume the true suchness (tathatā).
That which can permeate where there is no place for permeation is therefore called "inconceivable permeation.
Furthermore, permeation is itself non-permeation.
The perfuming that is not [actually] perfumed is called inconceivable perfuming.
Regarding inconceivable transformation:
it refers to the mind of True Suchness receiving the perfuming of ignorance.
That which is immutable undergoes transformation;
therefore, it is called "inconceivable transformation.
Furthermore, transformation is itself non-transformation.
The transformation of that which is immutable is called the inconceivable transformation;
as stated in the Śrīmālā-sūtra, it is "stained while remaining unstained."
"Being stained yet unstained,
difficult to comprehend" refers to this inconceivable [nature].
However, because this perfuming and transformation are extremely subtle and hidden,
the manifest consciousnesses that arise have subtle and fine modes of activity (*ākāra*);
within these, there are also the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).

Since it mentions the coarse while including the subtle, it is simply called the "manifesting consciousness" (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*); this is precisely the non-corresponding mind (*asamprayukta-citta*).
As for "grasping various objects" (*viṣaya-grahaṇa*):

This is because the various objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (ādarśa-vijñāna) are able to stir that ocean of mind, giving rise to the waves of the various active consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna).
Regarding "the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization":
within that ocean of the mind where [all things] are in conjunction,
the habitual tendencies of false thoughts have been perfuming it continuously since time immemorial.
Because one has never been free from thought,
these objects and thoughts perfuming and stirring the ocean of the mind give rise to various consciousnesses;
for both deluded thought and the objects are coarse and manifest.
The manifesting consciousness of discrimination (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) has coarse and manifest modes of activity that constitute the associated mind (*samprayukta-citta*).
In the sutra, it is intended to clarify that the manifesting consciousness arises because it depends upon inconceivable perfuming (*vāsanā*).
It abides by virtue of inconceivable transformation.
The event-consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna) arises in dependence upon objects and abides in dependence upon the ocean of mind.
In this treatise, only the conditions for arising are discussed;
therefore, the basis for abiding is not addressed.
Thus, regarding the subtle [level], only the permeation by ignorance is mentioned.
In the coarse [level], only the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is mentioned. Second, within the section that reveals the meaning of cessation through inversion, there are two parts:
first, the formal exposition;
second, the resolution of doubts.
"If the cause ceases, then the condition ceases"—this consists of two parts.
First, it clarifies universal cessation:
that is, when ignorance is extinguished through the attainment of its antidote.
The objective realm of the manifesting consciousness (*nirmāṇa-vijñāna*) that arises from ignorance also ceases accordingly;
thus it is said that "when the cause ceases, the conditions cease.
Because the cause ceases, the non-associated mind ceases; because the conditions cease, the associated mind ceases. This is the second section, specifically revealing cessation.
Regarding the prior cessation of causes:
because the three subtle states arise based closely upon the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*),
when ignorance ceases, they also cease accordingly.
Regarding those that subsequently cease through conditions:
because they arise by depending on the proximate objective conditions of the three coarse defilements,
they also cease when their objective fields cease.
This is based on the principle of beginning and end, arising and ceasing, to clarify the meaning of the two kinds of production and extinction;
it does not concern the meaning of momentary production and extinction. [End of section] "Dispelling Doubts."
First the question, then the answer. The question asks:
"If the mind ceases, how can there be continuity? If there is continuity, how can you speak of ultimate cessation? Within this question, it says: "If the mind ceases, how can there be continuity?"
If the substance of the mind were to perish when its objects perish,
then the substance of the mind would have already perished even though the three subtle states of ignorance had not yet been exhausted.
Furthermore, by relying on what dharma does this mind associated with doubt continue its succession?
And if it continues, how is it ultimately extinguished?
If it is said that because the essence of the mind is imperishable,
ignorance is enabled to continue in succession,
then since the essence of the mind is indeed imperishable...
If ignorance is constantly continuous,
how can the path of practice achieve its ultimate cessation?
This doubt is an incongruous state of mind.
In the response, both of these are answered together. Regarding the presence of the dharma, the metaphor, and their application:

The answer is: That which is called "extinction" refers only to the extinction of the mind’s manifestations, not the extinction of the mind’s essence. Regarding the statement that only the manifestations of the mind are extinguished and not its essence: it means that when objects of perception are extinguished, [the mind remains].
It is only the coarse characteristics of mind that cease;
it is not the essential nature of mind itself that ceases.
Furthermore, when ignorance ceases, [the coarse characteristics of mind cease].
"Only the subtle characteristics of mind are extinguished,
yet the essence of mind is not extinguished.
This is a comprehensive answer to both questions.
These two are specifically illustrated in the analogy:

just as wind exists in dependence upon water and possesses the characteristic of movement, if the water were to cease, then the characteristic of wind would be severed and have no basis for support. Since the water does not cease, the characteristic of wind continues; it is only when the wind ceases that the characteristic of movement also ceases accordingly, not because the water ceases. Thus, "just as wind moves in dependence upon water."
This metaphor shows that because the wind of ignorance relies upon the substance of the mind, it possesses the characteristic of movement;
it demonstrates that apart from the substance of the mind, ignorance cannot manifest the characteristic of movement on its own.
"If the water were extinguished" means that there would be no basis for reliance whatsoever.
This demonstrates that if the substance of the mind were to perish when the object and its fruit perish,
then the wind of ignorance would have nothing to move.
The three subtle states, such as karma and so forth,
should then be extinguished; yet water does not extinguish the continuity of wind because when the objective sphere ceases, the essence of the mind does not cease.
The three subtle states of ignorance thus achieve long-term continuity.
This is because when ignorance ceases, the objective realm ceases;
it is not that the objective realm ceases and thereby ignorance ceases.
For this reason,
when the objective sphere ceases,
the mind is stirred by ignorance.
"The three subtle [states] continue in succession.
This answers the first question regarding the meaning of the cessation of the corresponding mind.
"Only the wind ceases, and so on, up to it is not the water that ceases."
When ignorance is exhausted,
the moving characteristics of karma and so forth also perish accordingly;
it is not that the essence of the tranquil mind perishes as well.
This response does not accord with the meaning of the cessation of the non-corresponding mind (*viprayukta-citta*).
In the synthesis, it sequentially synthesizes the two preceding types of mind. Ignorance (*avidyā*) likewise moves based upon the substance of the mind;

if the substance of the mind were to cease, sentient beings would be cut off and have no basis for support. Because the substance does not cease, the mind attains continuity. It is only because delusion (*moha*) ceases that the characteristics of the mind follow in cessation, but it is not the case that the cognitive wisdom of the mind (*citta-jñāna*) ceases. As for "it is not the case that the cognitive wisdom of the mind ceases":
In the preceding passage, it was called "awakening" (jue) because it is contrasted with "non-awakening" (bujue);
thus, a single consciousness possesses two meanings.
Now, it is called "wisdom" (zhi) because it is contrasted with "delusion" (chi).
Thus, the one mind possesses both essence and characteristics;
when the characteristics of non-awakening and delusion are extinguished, they transform into initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*),
yet the essence of the wisdom of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) does not perish.
This is non-dual and indistinguishable from the return to the source.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the characteristics of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of defilement and purity.
From here on, the second part clarifies how defilement and purity mutually permeate and give rise to one another in an uninterrupted succession.
This immediately clarifies the meaning of the aforementioned general section on how all phenomena are produced.
Within this, there are four parts;
first, the number is stated to provide a general heading.
First, the names of the defiled and pure dharmas are listed;
second, the meaning of the perfuming of defilement and purity is explained in detail;
third, the meaning of the exhaustion and non-exhaustion of defilement and purity is clarified.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas which, by virtue of the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*), cause defiled and pure dharmas to arise without interruption. Regarding the first and second [of these], it is because they mutually support one another through their defiled and pure characteristics that their arising occurs without interruption.

What are the four? First, pure phenomena are called *tathatā* (suchness). Second, all causes of defilement are called ignorance (*avidyā*). Third, the deluded mind is called the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*). Fourth, deluded objects, namely the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Regarding the second point, it is said that pure phenomena are called *tathatā*.
This is the True Suchness within the gate of arising and ceasing.
It is called "pure phenomena" for three reasons.
First, with respect to its essence.
First, because it is pure from the beginning;
second, regarding its essence and characteristics,
because of internal permeation.
This is because it causes that which is defiled to return to its original purity.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) from the Liang dynasty states:
"That which is capable of establishing [the proof]..."

That which is established refers to the ten kinds of newly arisen correct practices, while that which establishes them refers to the ten kinds of dharmas of the qualities of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Third, because it perfumes through its function,
it forms a pure condition in accordance with the capacity of the recipient.
As for the defiled cause being named ignorance (*avidyā*):
This refers to the six defilements, the nine characteristics, and so forth;
all exist because of ignorance. The deluded mind encompasses both the object-consciousness (*viṣayavijñāna*) and the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Now, based on its fundamental nature,
it is simply called "karmic consciousness.
As for the delusory objects, they refer to the six sense-fields.
This refers to the objects perceived by the *pravṛtti-vijñāna*; these three are all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*).

Because these defiled phenomena possess distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*) that depend upon causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they are fully explained as being of three types.
Although pure dharmas and defiled dharmas establish the meaning of mutual perfuming, their essence and function have never been distinct.
Therefore, only one type is clarified [in the following]. Within the extensive explanation, there are two parts.
First the general, then the specific.
Within the general section, there are two parts:
first the analogy, then the application.

Regarding the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*): it is like a worldly garment which, though actually devoid of fragrance, comes to possess a scent when perfumed by someone with incense; this is likewise so. The pure *tathatā* is actually devoid of defilement, yet because it is perfumed by ignorance, the appearance of defilement arises. The defiled phenomena of ignorance are actually devoid of pure activity, yet because they are perfumed by *tathatā*, the function of purity arises. [This concludes] the second section within the "Conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
This refers to the perfuming of defilement and purity.

To say that there are defiled characteristics because of perfuming is to show that while the Truth (Tathatā) is itself without characteristics, it manifests characteristics in accordance with perfuming.
Furthermore, it reveals that false dharmas have no substantial essence;
therefore, they are merely called "characteristics.
Moreover, these characteristics themselves lack the functional capacity for the reversal of the flow [of consciousness].
Therefore, it speaks of "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) and not of "function" (vṛtti).
This is explained according to the gate of arising and ceasing that follows the flow [of phenomena].
This interprets the passage in the sutra concerning how the Tathāgatagarbha is perfumed by evil habits and so forth.
Second, regarding that which has the function of purification:
this is the true suchness of original enlightenment within the gate of arising and ceasing;
therefore, it possesses the meaning of perfuming.
Within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), however, this meaning does not apply.
It is because of this internal permeation of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya) upon non-enlightenment that it causes the arising of weariness with saṃsāra and the seeking of liberation.
Flowing back toward and conforming with the Truth is therefore called "function.
This explains the scriptural passage stating that because the *tathāgatagarbha* exists, one is able to feel weary of the suffering of birth and death.
This refers to the joyful seeking of nirvāṇa.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because of the power of the future Buddha-nature inherent in those of icchantika nature..."
They will again give rise to wholesome roots.
What is called the power of Buddha-nature is precisely this power of internal permeation of original enlightenment.
This is because a single consciousness contains these two meanings,
as they mutually perfuse one another to universally produce both defilement and purity.
Herein, "Buddha" means awakening.
Nature is the fundamental basis;
therefore, Buddha-nature is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*). From here below, in the second section, the detailed explanation, there are two parts:
first, the defiled, and second, the pure.
Within the defiled [aspect] there are also two:

How is it that the perfuming which gives rise to defiled phenomena is uninterrupted? Generally speaking, there are two kinds of perfuming.
First is habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*),
which refers to the perfuming of the substance of the mind so that it becomes defiled, pure, and so forth.
Second is supportive perfuming (*upastambha-vāsanā*).
This refers to the mutual support between the functioning mind and its objects, as well as the various afflictions, and so forth.

Specifically, because there is ignorance based upon the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, that ignorance—which is the cause of defiled dharmas—infuses the *tathatā*. Because of this infusion, a deluded mind arises. Because the deluded mind exists, it infuses ignorance; failing to comprehend the *tathatā* dharma, non-awakening thoughts arise, manifesting delusive objects. Because these delusive objects—which are the conditions for defiled dharmas—exist, they infuse the deluded mind, causing it to become attached through thought and to create various karmas, thereby undergoing all manner of physical and mental suffering. Regarding the initial statement, "based upon *tathatā*, there is ignorance": *(Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding the explanation of the first point.)*
This refers to the essence of both the perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka-dharma*) and the perfumed object (*kṣobhya-dharma*).
Furthermore, one might argue that here only the perfuming agent, ignorance (*avidyā*), is mentioned;
however, because it must necessarily rely upon the True [Nature], it is mentioned by way of its fundamental basis.
"Because there is ignorance, up to its permeating the True Suchness (tathatā)" refers to the meaning of the permeation by fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā).
"Because of this permeation, there is the deluded mind" means:
Based on the perfuming of ignorance, the True Suchness is stirred, giving rise to the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna).

By means of this deluded mind, it in turn provides the conditions for the perfuming of ignorance, increasing its lack of understanding and causing it to transform into the evolving consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna) and the manifesting consciousness (darśana-vijñāna).
Therefore it is said: because non-awakening causes thoughts to arise and manifest delusive objects;

by means of these objects, the ocean of the mind is further perfumed and stirred, giving rise to the waves of the various consciousnesses which take those objects as their conditions and focus upon them.
This refers to the arising of the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness).
Among the six types of coarseness (*audārya*),
the first two are termed "recollection" (*smṛti*).
The middle two are called "fettering" (saṃyojana).
The latter two are named the same as these.
This means that karma is created based on the afflictions (kleśa).
"Receiving the retribution of suffering based on karma. From here below is the detailed explanation, which clarifies the aforementioned three types;

Regarding the meaning of this deluded realm’s perfuming, there are two kinds. What are these two? First, the perfuming that increases conceptualization; second, the perfuming that increases grasping. As for the increase of conceptualization:

This refers to the proliferation of the conceptualization of dharmas (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*)— which consists of the characteristics of wisdom and the characteristics of continuity within the *pravṛttivijñāna* (active consciousness)— due to the power of objects.
As for "the proliferation of grasping":
Within the increasing consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*), there is the grasping of signs and the conceptualization of names;
this refers to the afflictions of the view of self (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) and craving.

Regarding the meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind (*vikalpa-citta*), there are two kinds. What are the two? First, the fundamental perfuming of the *karma-vijñāna*, which causes one to undergo the suffering of birth and death (*utpāda-nirodha*) as an Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, or any Bodhisattva. Second, the perfuming of the increasing discriminative consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*), which causes one to undergo the suffering of karmic bondage as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Within the perfuming of the deluded mind...
Regarding the fundamental habituation of the karma-consciousness:
because this karma-consciousness can support and perfuse the ignorance of the dwelling stage (ālayavijñāna),
it is deluded regarding the signless (animitta).
It can give rise to the continuity of evolving characteristics (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) and manifesting characteristics (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*),
causing those followers of the three vehicles, although they have emerged from the triple world and departed from the coarse suffering of the segmented consciousness of objects (*vastu-vijñāna*),
to still undergo the *ālayavijñāna*’s suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
However, this subtle suffering has existed since beginningless time;
it is merely described in terms of its manifest state at the time one has already abandoned coarse suffering, in order to distinguish the subtle from the coarse.
Regarding the perfuming by the event-consciousness (*saviṣaya-vijñāna*): this event-consciousness is able to support and perfume the arising of ignorance at the time [of rebirth],
giving rise to coarse afflictions such as views and craving.
One initiates actions of body and speech to create various karmas, thereby undergoing the suffering of the mundane, segmented existence of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Regarding the meaning of the permeation of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*), there are two kinds. What are these two? First, fundamental permeation, because it has the function of accomplishing the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*); second, the permeation of views and craving that arises therefrom, because it has the function of accomplishing the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*). Within this permeation of ignorance...

"Fundamental perfuming" refers to fundamental non-awakening (mūla-abodhi) perfuming and stirring True Suchness (tathatā) to form the various consciousnesses, such as karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and so forth. However,
because we are citing the very first here, it is called "karma-consciousness."
Regarding that which is perfumed by the arising of views and attachments:
this refers to the perfuming of the non-awakening of the secondary branches upon the essence of the mind, thereby forming the discerning consciousness of phenomena (*vijñapti-vijñāna*).
As stated in the preceding text:
Because this consciousness grows by depending on the afflictions of views and craving,
it is said to be "that which arises," since the derivative follows from the fundamental.
This is stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
