How does the perfuming that gives rise to pure dharmas proceed without interruption? It is because the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) exists that it can perfume ignorance; by the power of the causes and conditions of this perfuming, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of saṃsāra and to joyfully seek nirvāṇa. Because this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of weariness and seeking, it in turn perfumes True Suchness. [This section consists of two parts.]
First, it is clarified that the internal permeation of True Suchness (tathatā) causes ignorance (avidyā) to produce pure karma;
subsequently, this very function of purity permeates back into True Suchness,
increasing its power.
The former refers to original perfuming;
the latter refers to new perfuming.
This can be seen in the relevant passages of the text. Regarding the "functional capacity" (kāritra):
The section on cause and effect has two parts.

Regarding the cause: having gained confidence in one’s own nature and realized that the mind is a deluded movement lacking any external objects, one practices the method of distancing oneself from them; because one knows with suchness that no external objects exist, one engages in concordant conduct through various skillful means—neither grasping nor conceptualizing—even until, by the power of long-term cultivation, [the realization is perfected]. This is the causal stage.
"Having already realized one's own nature" refers to the faith within the stage of the ten faiths.
"Knowing that the mind is falsely stirred," and so forth, follows below.
This refers to the practice during the stage of the Three Worthies.
To know that the mind's false movement has no external object is understanding.
One who cultivates the dharma of seclusion relies on understanding to establish practice; that is to say,
it consists of the contemplations such as thorough investigation.
This refers to the practice of [realizing] that consciousness alone exists and there are no external objects.
To say that one knows, as it truly is, the absence of objects means that on the first bhūmi,
during the path of seeing, one realizes the principle of vijñaptimātra (consciousness-only).
Because it differs from the previous inferential contemplation, it is called "knowing as it truly is.
Regarding the passage from "various" down to "the power of long-term perfuming," this clarifies how,
within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one extensively cultivates the myriad practices to skillfully manifest True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Not grasping" means that there are no characteristics to be grasped.
"Not recollecting" means...
That which can be contemplated as non-arising over a long duration is due to the cultivation [of wisdom] throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. From here below, the fruit is elucidated.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the cessation of delusions;
second, the realization of principle.

Ignorance is extinguished; because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise. Because there is no arising, objects of perception are accordingly extinguished. Since causes and conditions are both extinguished, the characteristics of the mind are entirely exhausted; this is called attaining nirvana and accomplishing spontaneous karma. [End of] the preceding section.
"The cessation of ignorance" means the exhaustion of fundamental ignorance.
Because ignorance has ceased, the mind does not arise.
The deluded mind is exhausted.
As for the cessation of the non-arising of objective realms,
it is the cessation of deluded objects.
This refers to the reversal of the three aforementioned types of defiled dharmas.
From "by causes and conditions" down to "spontaneous karma," it clarifies the qualities of the realized Dharma (*dharmatā*).
The cause refers to ignorance;
the condition refers to delusive objects;
and the mental characteristic refers to the defiled mind.
Because these are all exhausted, the transformation of the basis of the mind’s essence is called attaining *nirvāṇa*.
The arising of inconceivable karmic functions is called "spontaneous activity" (*svayambhū-karman*). Below this, there are two sections in the extensive explanation.
First, the perfuming of the deluded mind is explained;
subsequently, the perfuming of True Suchness is revealed.
Within the former, there is both a heading and an explanation.

The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are the two? First, the perfuming of the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), which pertains to ordinary people and those of the Two Vehicles who, weary of the suffering of birth and death, gradually advance toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities. In the commentary, "the discriminative consciousness of phenomena" refers precisely to the aforementioned mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because this consciousness does not know that all objects are merely consciousness,
it clings to the notion that there are truly existent external realms.
Although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles may give rise to the resolve to head toward liberation, [they remain bound by this misconception].
Yet they still calculate that there is birth and death to be weary of and nirvana to be delighted in;
they do not understand the principle that all is but mind,
and thus continue to act by the power of this mental attention.
After a long time, they will again attain bodhi;
therefore it is said that the perfuming of the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna* (the consciousness of discriminating phenomena) leads gradually toward the unsurpassed path.

Second is the perfuming of the *manas* (the mental faculty), which refers to how various bodhisattvas resolve with courageous vigor to swiftly proceed toward nirvana. Regarding this perfuming of the *manas*:
If discussed in terms of its fundamental nature,
it is called the "karmic consciousness" (karma-vijñāna); yet, when considered from a broader perspective:
This refers precisely to the aforementioned five kinds of mentation (*manas*).
Because all bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are merely the manifestations of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*),
they abandon the conceptualization of external objects as real entities, which is the discrimination of the object-consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*).
Having realized that all is mind-only,
one proceeds toward the principle with rapidity;
because this differs from the gradual awakening mentioned previously, it is said that "one swiftly proceeds even unto nirvana."
Question: Since, in this context, the deluded mind arises through simultaneous perfuming of the True Suchness and subsequently flows forth,
and since mental perfuming belongs to the ālayavijñāna,
how can each [individual] independently resolve to cultivate practice?
Answer: The aforementioned ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not awaken to the *ālayavijñāna*.
Rather, they resolve their minds and engage in practice by relying solely on the sustaining power of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of discriminating phenomena).
Because they do not penetrate the fundamental source,
they are distant and remote from great bodhi.
Therefore, it is called "gradual.
Since this bodhisattva has already realized the *ālaya-vijñāna*,
they rely upon the sustaining power of this very consciousness.
Only then can one resolve to practice;
because of having realized the fundamental nature, one draws near to great bodhi.
Therefore, it is said to be "swift.

This explains the perfuming (*vāsanā*) by way of the mutual support of the bases (*āśraya*), rather than through each [basis] independently generating the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and so forth.
This is as explained below in the section on "Evidence for the Arising of the Mind. Regarding the permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are three parts:
first, the enumeration of the number;
second, the listing of the names.
This refers to internal permeation and external conditions.
Third, the analysis of characteristics,
which contains two parts.
First, there is an individual explanation;
later, there is a combined clarification.
Within the former, there are also two parts.
First is the essence and characteristics;
second is the greatness of function.
Within the former, there are also two parts.
The first part correctly reveals [the doctrine],
while the latter removes doubts.
Within the former, the cultivation (vāsanā) is first analyzed.

The meaning of the permeation (*vāsanā*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is twofold. What are the two? First, the permeation of its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*); second, the permeation of its functional activity (*vṛtti*). Regarding the permeation of its own essential nature: from beginningless time, it has been endowed with untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and possesses the nature of inconceivable activity that serves as an objective sphere. Based on these two meanings, there is constant permeation; because this power is effective, it can cause sentient beings to weary of the suffering of birth and death, to joyfully seek nirvana, and to have confidence in their own bodies as possessing the dharma of True Suchness, thereby giving rise to the resolve for practice. As for the phrase "from beginningless time" up to "inconceivable activity": [it refers to the fact that] from the very beginningless past, the nature of True Suchness has been inherently endowed with the seeds of all pure dharmas and the capacity for inconceivable transformative functions. Because these two aspects—being endowed with the seeds of pure dharmas and possessing the capacity for inconceivable functions—constantly permeate one another, they serve as the internal cause for the arising of the bodhicitta. This is called the "permeation of the essential nature. By virtue of this permeation, sentient beings come to realize that within their own bodies there exists the dharma of True Suchness, and thus they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and engage in spiritual cultivation.
The fundamental awakening of non-emptiness is called the outflow-free dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*).
This dharma secretly permeates sentient beings;
it is not something that can be apprehended by the ordinary mind.
Therefore, it is called "inconceivable karma.
Herein, "karma" refers to the function of mysterious permeation.
Regarding "acting as the nature of the objective realm":
this clarifies that it does not merely permeate that deluded mind to cause it to develop weariness with and seek after [liberation], thereby forming the contemplative wisdom;
rather, it also serves as the objective realm for that contemplative wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "by means of these two dharmas, etc.," the following clarifies the function of perfuming (*vāsanā*):
that is to say, these two dharmas of mind and object—
or alternatively, these two dharmas of essence and characteristic.
Because the latent influence upon sentient beings possesses power,
it causes them to give rise to practices such as revulsion and seeking.
Regarding "confidence in oneself" and so forth:
This clarifies the characteristics of practice arising based on perfuming. Regarding the "Dispelling of Doubts," there are two parts:
first the question, then the answer. The question asks:

If this is the meaning—that all sentient beings possess *tathatā* (Suchness) and so forth, and all are perfumed—why is there a distinction between those with faith and those without faith, and why are there immeasurable differences in priority and sequence? Why should they not all simultaneously realize for themselves that they possess the *tathatā*-dharma, diligently cultivate skillful means, and enter *nirvāṇa* at once? [End of Question]
The former is based on the presence or absence of present faith,
while the latter is based on the sequence of future faith; since the internal permeation is equal in both cases, [the result is the same].
How can it be so? All [the points] should be brought together at once to form the objection.
This is an objection that clings to the particular while doubting the general.

The answer is: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally one, yet from the very beginning there have been immeasurable and boundless afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā*), whose intrinsic natures differ in their degrees of thickness and thinness. Therefore, the various higher afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges arise based on ignorance; the various afflictions of self-view, attachment, and defilement also arise based on ignorance. Because all such afflictions arise depending on ignorance and possess infinite distinctions of sequence and type that only a Tathāgata can know, [the answer] consists of two parts.
The first sentence clarifies throughout that internal permeation is not non-existent;
the latter clarifies that defilement and purity depend upon conditions,
thereby manifesting the sequence of the preceding and following sections.
This passage consists of two parts.
The first concerns defiled afflictions,
which vary in their intensity depending on the conditions of dependent origination.
Subsequently, regarding the pure dharmas,
they rely on conditions that differ before and after; thus,
while there is discourse concerning the former, there are immeasurable [factors] up to their being not identical.

This refers to the fundamental stage of ignorance (*mūla-avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), whose intrinsic nature and its various manifestations differ according to the degree of spiritual capacity in individuals;
those with a thick [affliction] lack faith,
while those with a thin [affliction] possess it.
The same applies to what precedes and follows.
It is not that internal perfuming causes it to be so.
As for the distinctions among the afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges that arise based on ignorance:
This refers to the ignorance regarding the phenomena and activities arising from nescience;
it is subsumed under the coarse portion of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
As for the afflictions of self-view and attachment:
These are the four abiding afflictions arising from ignorance;
they are subsumed under the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Thus, the following pair concludes the discussion of the two preceding types of affliction.
All arise based on fundamental ignorance;
for this reason, they are not identical from beginning to end.
Thus, the distinctions among the natures of these afflictions are immeasurable.
The sequence of before and after is difficult to discern;
therefore, only a Buddha can fully comprehend it. [The passage below] clarifies that pure dharmas exist with a temporal sequence because they depend upon conditions.

Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas have causes and conditions; only when causes and conditions are fully assembled are they accomplished and realized. If there were only internal causes without relying on external conditions, [they could not be established].
It may be as you have criticized.
However, it is only through the external application of perfuming (*vāsanā*) and the internal primary cause that [the result] can be fully accomplished.
Therefore, there is a sequence of before and after;
they cannot exist simultaneously.
For this reason, the text above opens with the two types of perfuming.
It does not say "one. Within this, there is the combination of the principle (dharma) and the metaphor (upamā).
In the section on the principle, it merely clarifies that when causes and conditions are complete, attainment is achieved;
it briefly omits the failure resulting from their incompleteness.
In the analogy, the fault of lacking [the conditions] is specifically clarified; it is stated briefly that there is no attainment without the complete set of conditions.
In the application, both meanings are explained together.

The meaning can be understood through the analogy. For example, the fire-nature within wood is the direct cause of fire; yet, if no one knows of it and it does not rely on expedient means, there is no possibility that it could spontaneously burn the wood. It is the same with sentient beings: although they possess the power of the direct cause as an internal perfuming influence, if they do not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to serve as external conditions, there is no possibility that they could spontaneously sever their afflictions and enter *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, even if they possess the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharma lacks the power of perfuming influence, they will be unable to ultimately weary of the suffering of birth and death or joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*. In this synthesis, "sentient beings" corresponds to the aforementioned "wood."
The true cause accords with the nature of fire;
if one does not encounter the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and so forth, it is as if there were no one to know it.
That it could spontaneously sever itself below and simultaneously spontaneously burn itself is impossible;
this demonstrates the fault of lacking conditions (*pratyaya*).
If, despite its existence, it is explained that it lacks the cause (*hetu*), then [the argument] is not established.
This means that for those whose ignorance is thick and heavy, although there is the internal permeation of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*),
they lack sufficient power; therefore,
even when encountering the external conditions of virtuous friends, [they remain unable to awaken].
Yet it is also unable to cause them to attain the Way.

This clarifies the fault of mutual deficiency in causes and conditions. Following this, the section beginning with "If causes and conditions are complete" clarifies the attainment through the correspondence of nature and function.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the analysis of the complete conditions;
second, the ability to give rise to the lower [stages], clarifying the permeation and benefit.

If the causes and conditions are fully present—namely, possessing the power of one's own habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) and being protected by the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—[the benefit occurs]. This is the second [section] on the benefits.
First, the self-benefit is clarified.
By means of cultivating roots of goodness, the subsequent stage of superior progress is clarified.

One is able to give rise to a mind of wearying detachment from suffering, believe in the existence of *nirvāṇa*, and cultivate roots of goodness. Because these cultivated roots of goodness reach maturity, one encounters Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provide instruction, benefit, and joy; thus, one is able to advance toward the path of *nirvāṇa*. They demonstrate its meaning and teach its practice.
This is because one attains the practice that accomplishes meaningful benefit and thereby gives rise to joy. Regarding the cultivation through application, there are two parts:
first, a general indication by citing specific instances; second, a detailed exposition according to conditions, beginning with the passage "In this way, external conditions... and so forth.
The three [sections] within the "Detailed Exposition" are: the heading, the enumeration, and the explanation.

Regarding the "power of external conditions for perfuming," this refers to the power of external conditions for sentient beings. Such external conditions have immeasurable meanings, but they are briefly explained as being of two kinds. What are these two? First, the differentiated condition; second, the equal condition. Within the enumeration, it says "differentiated condition."
It serves as a condition for the perfuming of consciousness regarding various minor matters;
that is to say, it is so called because its manifested forms are diverse.
Alternatively, it may also serve as a condition for those with diverse capacities.
This means that those from the three stages of worthiness upward, up to all Buddhas, are able to act as this condition.
As for the "equal condition," it acts as a condition for the karmic consciousness-impressions (*karma-vijñāna-vāsanā*) of all Bodhisattvas.
This means that because the manifested bodies of the Buddhas are exclusively equal and non-dual;
it may also mean that they serve as the condition for sentient beings with minds of equality.
This refers to those from the first bhūmi upward, up to all Buddhas.
It must rely on the power of the wisdom of identical essence to function as this condition. Regarding the commentary, there are two parts;
the condition itself is divided into two sections.
Within the first section, there are two further divisions.
First the general, then the specific.
Within the general section there are also two parts;
first, the cause that brings about the functional response.
Later, [the text] may serve as a subordinate section to correctly clarify the characteristics of its application.

Regarding the "distinctive conditions": this person relies upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, from the initial generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood; throughout this interval, they either see them or keep them in mind. Within the preceding section, the phrase "this person" refers to this individual.
For those whose faculties and desires are such,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest as external conditions and essences.
From "from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment" onwards,
it clarifies the period of practicing to respond to the conditions and capacities [of sentient beings].
Regarding "whether seeing or recollecting":
This clearly explains how the mind of the practitioner serves as the vessel for the manifestation of the response.
That is to say, it refers to beholding their physical form and recollecting their meritorious virtues.
Within the section on the application of signs, there are two parts.
First, the primary clarification of the function of differentiation;
second, from "arousing great compassion" onwards, the discernment of the benefits of that function.

[This section] may manifest as kinsmen, parents, or various relatives; or as servants; or as friends; or as enemies; or it may initiate the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). Within the former [section], there are two parts.
The first five phrases expand the general into the particular;
the subsequent section, ending with "down to," subsumes the particular back into the general.
Regarding these five phrases:
First, one gathers living beings through loving-kindness;
second, one attracts others by occupying a humble position;
third, one encourages and inspires them by being of their own kind.
Fourth, one causes them to enter the Path by means of instilling fear in them.
Fifth, one directly gathers them through the four methods and causes them to practice for their own benefit;
the text is clear on this point.

Furthermore, by means of the power of the habitual perfuming of great compassion—which arises from all the immeasurable conditions of his various deeds—he enables sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness, so that they may obtain benefit through either seeing or hearing him. This section on the specific distinctions has two parts.
First, based on whether the faculties are mature or immature, two conditions—proximate and remote—are distinguished.
Subsequently, each of these proximate and remote conditions is further divided into two.
Each division includes both a heading and an explanation.

These conditions are of two kinds. What are the two? First, the proximate condition, by which one attains liberation quickly; second, the remote condition, by which one attains liberation after a long period. Furthermore, these two—proximate and remote conditions—are each divided into two types. What are the two? First, the condition for increasing practice; second, the condition for receiving the Path. Regarding the latter, as for the condition for increasing practice:
This refers to the practice of skillful means,
which is one's own portion; it is that by which the recipient of the Way [attains realization].
This refers to the superior progress that corresponds to correct contemplation based on the aforementioned preliminary means;
it may also be understood as the practice of benefiting others through the four means of attraction from the very beginning.
This is because it subsequently constitutes the practice for one's own benefit through the three types of emptiness. Regarding the impartial condition (*samatā-pratyaya*), there are two parts.
First, to clarify the acting condition (*kāraṇa-hetu*):
as for the impartial condition, it refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

All vow to deliver all sentient beings, spontaneously perfuming them through constant and eternal non-abandonment; by virtue of the power of the wisdom of identical essence, they manifest karmic activities according to how beings see and hear them. Among these, the vow to deliver sentient beings is as follows:
It is the mind of equanimity.
As for "naturally equal," it constantly accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
"By means of the power of the wisdom of the identical essence" explains the constant functioning.
"In accordance with what is appropriate," and so forth.
Revealing its functional characteristics. II. Clarifying the meaning of equality as manifested in response to capacities.
This means that sentient beings rely upon samādhi to attain the equal vision of all Buddhas; that is to say, bodhisattvas from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) onward rely on the power of samādhi.
One sees that the dimensions of all Buddhas' bodies are equal,
without any marks of distinction between self and other;
therefore, it is called "seeing with equality."
The preceding section has concluded the detailed explanation of essence and function. From here on is the second part, which provides a combined explanation based on persons.
This consists of two sections:
the heading and the explanation.

This differentiation of the perfuming of essence and function further consists of two kinds. What are these two? First, that which is not yet in correspondence, referring to ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds; because they perfume [the mind] by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are able to practice through the power of faith. Second, within the explanation, there are also two [further categories].
First, regarding the three [types of persons] who have not yet attained correspondence,
the first section identifies the individuals according to their stages;
the second distinguishes the inferiority of their practice.
The subsequent section clarifies that which is not yet associated:
among the practices, there is the perfuming by the mental consciousness of ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners,
and the perfuming by the five types of mind of Bodhisattvas.
One has not yet realized True Suchness (tathatā);
therefore, it is said that one practices based on faith.

Because one has not yet attained a non-conceptual mind that accords with the essence, one has not yet attained the practice of sovereign karma that accords with its function. Within this state of non-correspondence, there are two [aspects].

The initial statement that one has not yet attained a non-conceptual mind corresponding to the essence clarifies that because one lacks the wisdom of the fundamental essence (*mūladharmakāya*), one has not yet corresponded with the body of the dharma-nature.
The subsequent statement refers to the fact that one lacks the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) which realizes the truth.
It has not yet attained correspondence with the functions of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.

Second, "already corresponding" refers to the *dharmakāya* Bodhisattvas who have attained non-conceptual mind and correspond with the self-essence of all Buddhas; they attain mastery over karma and correspond with the cognitive functions of all Buddhas, practicing spontaneously by relying solely on the power of the Dharma, perfuming *tathatā*, and thereby extinguishing ignorance. Within this second section on "already corresponding," there are also three [subdivisions].
First, the stage of the person is revealed;
this refers to bodhisattvas on the bhūmis.
Next, the actual correspondence is correctly established.
To attain the non-conceptual mind means that the wisdom of suchness (yathābhūta-jñāna) is in accord with its essence.
To be in accord with the functional activity of the Buddha's wisdom means...
This means that it is so because of the possession of suchness-measuring wisdom (*yathāvadbhāvikatājñāna*).
The latter clarifies the excellence of its practice:
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one practices having realized the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
This is not like the preceding stages where there is only the power of faith; therefore, it is said that one "relies on the power of the Dharma.
As for "spontaneous cultivation," this refers to the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) from the eighth stage onward.
The perfuming of the True [Mind] extinguishes the delusory;
this clarifies the completion of the practice.
Having finished explaining the perfuming of the Pure Dharma, the first section has been specifically elucidated above.
Next is the combined explanation.

This concludes the general clarification of the third point, the meaning of the perfuming of defilement and purity. Below this begins the fourth section, which clarifies the meaning of exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
This section contains two parts.

First, it is explained that defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) contradict reality, having no beginning but an end; subsequently, it is explained that pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) accord with principle, having a beginning but no end.

Furthermore, defiled phenomena have been continuously perfumed since time immemorial and continue until the attainment of Buddhahood, after which they are severed. Within pure phenomena, there are two [aspects].
The first part clearly reveals [the meaning], while the latter provides an explanatory proof.

Regarding the statement that the perfuming of pure dharmas has no exhaustion in the future: how is this principle established? It is because the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes [the mind], whereby the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharma-body manifests; and because the arising of activity through perfuming ensures there is no interruption. This is the explanatory proof.
This is because the perfuming of the True [Mind] extinguishes the delusory,
and its pure function is inexhaustible;
this can be seen in the relevant passages of the text.

The preceding section concludes the explanation of the dharmas that can manifest the meaning within the gate of arising and ceasing. From here on, the second part explains the great meaning manifested within the gate of arising and ceasing.
This contains two sections.
First, the two great [aspects] of essence and characteristic are explained;
subsequently, the greatness of function is analyzed individually.
Within the former, there are also two parts.
First, the two great names are presented as a general heading;
second, the two great meanings are explained in detail. Within the explanation of the meanings, there are likewise two parts.
First, the meaning of the greatness of essence is clarified.

Furthermore, as for the self-nature and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā): it is without increase or decrease among all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas; it is not born in the past limit and does not perish in the future limit, being ultimately eternal and constant. This means that although people may be distinguished by their status into superior or inferior categories, [True Suchness remains unchanged].
The true essence conforms to people without ever increasing or decreasing;
therefore, it is said to be without increase or decrease.
It is not that which is prior, nor even that which is eternally constant.
This reveals the reason why there is neither increase nor decrease:
it is "eternal" because it is not born at a prior limit,
and it is "constant" because it does not perish at a subsequent limit.

The stage of ordinary beings constitutes the prior limit, while the fruit of Buddhahood constitutes the posterior limit. From "From the origin" (*pūrvamūla*) onwards, the "Greatness of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamahattva*) is explained;
herein there are two parts.
First, the nature and virtues are clearly elucidated;
second, they are further distinguished through questions and answers.
Within the former, there are also two parts.
First, the characteristics of the virtues are clarified;
second, the establishment of the name is revealed.
Within the former [section], there are three parts.
First is the general [statement], next is the specific, and finally is the conclusion.
From the very beginning, its intrinsic nature is fully endowed with all virtues; this consists of six phrases within the specific section.

That is to say: because its own essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light; because it has the meaning of universally illuminating the dharma-realm; because it has the meaning of true and authentic cognition; because it has the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind; because it has the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; because it has the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty; [and] because it has the meaning of the primordial awakening of wisdom and clarity.
1. The meaning of the two types of awakening illuminating all phenomena; 2.
The meaning of being non-erroneous at the time of illumination; 3.
The meaning of the nature being free from the defilement of afflictions.
The meaning of the five nature-endowed virtues being perfectly complete;
the meaning of the nature-endowed virtues being immutable.

Because it possesses such qualities—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—which are inseparable, uninterrupted, non-different, and inconceivable, and because it is even fully satisfied with nothing lacking, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and also the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*. This concludes the section below.
This means that the sands of the Buddha-nature's virtues do not depart from the true essence; hence it is said they "do not depart.
Because they have continued uninterruptedly since beginningless time, it is said they are "uninterrupted."
It may also be said that the path of cultivation (pratipad) has not perished.
Because it shares the same flavor as the essence (dharmatā), it is called "not different.
Because this non-difference possesses the significance of the sands of the Ganges, it is called "inconceivable" (acintya).
Only the Buddha has fully realized and mastered it;
therefore, it is called the "Buddha-dharma.
It may also be said that this is the dharma that is to be awakened to.
If this true essence lacked the quality of nature,
the Tathāgata would not possess all qualities upon realizing it; yet,
having realized its nature, his myriad virtues are perfected.
This verifies that True Suchness (Tathatā) is inherently endowed with virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, it is said to be "complete and lacking nothing.
Below, two names are established.
In its hidden state, it is able to give birth to the Tathāgata and is thus called the *tathāgatagarbha*;
in its manifest state, it serves as the locus for the myriad virtues and is therefore named the *dharmakāya*. Below, there is a further analysis in two parts.
First, there is the objection based on the doubt that the essence and its characteristics are distinct; second, there is the response that the characteristics do not contradict the essence. Question:

It was stated above that the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) is equal and free from all characteristics; why, then, is it further said that this essence possesses such various kinds of meritorious qualities? Answer: Although these meanings of various meritorious qualities truly exist, they lack any characteristic of differentiation; they are identical in a single flavor, being only true suchness. Why is this so? Because it is non-discriminative and free from the characteristics of discrimination, it is therefore non-dual. The answer consists of two parts.
The first part clarifies that although there are distinctions, they are non-dual;
the latter part further clarifies, by means of what meaning,
that although they are non-dual, there are distinctions.
The preceding section also has two parts.
First, it clarifies that although actual virtues are numerous, they share the single flavor of suchness.
Second, it explains and establishes their non-duality.
"By means of non-conceptualization," because it is not that which performs conceptualization;
"free from the marks of conceptualization."
Because it is not an object of conceptual discrimination.
Next, because there is neither subject nor object of discrimination, it is non-dual. Within this non-duality and differentiation, first comes the brief [explanation], followed by the detailed one.
Furthermore, by what principle can distinctions be spoken of? It is shown by relying on the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the *karmic consciousness*.
A doubt arises within the summary: "Since they are non-dual, why speak of distinctions?"
The commentary states:
Based upon the infinitely numerous defiled dharmas that are the marks of the evolving consciousness,
this representation in reverse indicates the infinitely numerous distinctions of the pure virtues of *tathatā*.
Furthermore, because this passage cites the root of defilement, it simply refers to it as "karmic consciousness" (karmavijñāna). Regarding the extensive explanation, there are two parts:
first, the inquiry concerning the characteristics of the manifestation of defilement;
second, the individual presentation of those defiled dharmas in contrast [to their counterparts].

How is this shown? It is because all phenomena are fundamentally only mind; in reality there is no thought, yet through the non-awakening of the deluded mind, thoughts arise and various objective realms are perceived; therefore, it is said that ignorance is the non-arising of the nature of mind, which is precisely the meaning of the light of great wisdom. This is because all phenomena, up to and including non-thought, [are thus established].
This raises the principle that is the object of delusion.
As for the phrase "there being a deluded mind," it means that delusion arises based upon the True [Suchness].
This refers to the failure to realize the beginning and end of subtle, coarse, and defiled minds.
Being about to explain purity,
he first cites its opposite— defilement— to manifest it by contrast.
The subsequent phrases are all analogous.
What is meant by "manifestation"? It refers to the arising of mental attention through the characteristics of the mind.
Because it is due to the non-awakening of ignorance,
one knows that the nature of the mind does not arise;
this is precisely the luminous wisdom of original awakening.
Therefore, it is said that this is the meaning of the light of great wisdom. If the mind gives rise to views, there will be the characteristic of non-seeing;

when the nature of the mind is free from views, it is precisely the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm. Regarding the phrase "if the mind gives rise to views," etc.: If the mind gives rise to views, there will be the characteristic of non-seeing. When the nature of the mind is free from views, it is precisely the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm. As for the phrase "if the mind gives rise to views," etc.: [the commentary continues].
The phrase "clarifying that deluded vision is not all-pervasive;
the nature of mind is free from such vision" reveals that true illumination is perfectly luminous.

"If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition and lacks intrinsic nature. Regarding "if the mind has movement, it is not true cognition," this clarifies that deluded consciousness is inverted knowledge;
by reversing this, one reveals true illumination which is non-inverted.
The phrase "having no intrinsic nature" clarifies that delusive defilement has no substantial reality;
to turn back from this is to manifest the intrinsically pure mind.
"Impermanent, not blissful, not self, and not pure; [subject to] feverish affliction, decay, and transformation, one lacks mastery.
Regarding these terms such as "impermanent," they clarify the four delusive losses; conversely, they reveal the four virtues of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because the various afflictions burn the mind and constitute extreme heat and distress,
True Suchness is said to be cool and refreshing.
The delusive defilements undergo transformation and change;
this is the characteristic of decay and alteration.
This, in turn, reveals that True Suchness (tathatā) is unchanging.
Because one is not autonomous due to being bound by the fruits of karma, it is revealed that True Suchness (tathatā) is autonomous.
Therefore, the preceding passage states: "Because its meaning is that of purity, immutability, and autonomy."

"Up to and including the possession of meanings of false defilements exceeding the sands of the Ganges—in contrast to these meanings, because the nature of the mind is unmoving, there is the manifestation of the meanings of the characteristics of pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges. Regarding the phrase "up to and including the possession of," etc.:
This collectively enumerates the manifold delusions and defilements;
because it is the opposite of these,
the nature of the mind is immovable.

This refers to the presence of qualities such as those of the sands of the Ganges. If the mind arises and perceives further phenomena that can be recollected, then there is a deficiency; however, these immeasurable merits of pure dharmas are themselves the single mind, wherein nothing further is recollected. Therefore, being complete, it is called the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgatagarbha. Regarding the phrase "if the mind arises and perceives further phenomena," etc.: it means that if the mind stirs and views prior dharmas as objects of recollection, one remains incomplete. When this pure dharma is present in its immeasurable merit, it is precisely the single mind, free from further mental activity; thus, in its fulfillment, it is named the Dharmakāya, the treasury of the Tathāgata. As for the statement "if the mind arises and perceives further phenomena," and so forth: [it explains that any mental stirring toward perceived objects constitutes a lack of perfection].
This clarifies that seeking outside of the deluded mind is insufficient.
Such dharmas as purity and so forth— [are likewise].
The luminous, pure, and perfect nature requires no external seeking;
thus the name [of this section] may be understood. Second, the Great Function.
This passage consists of two parts.
First is the general explanation;
next, "This function has two [aspects]" and below is the specific explanation.
Within the former, there are also two parts.
First, the cause is presented in relation to the fruit;
second, the fruit is revealed by restating the cause.

Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness (tathatā), it refers to how the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, while originally on the causal ground, gave rise to great compassion, cultivated the various pāramitās, and gathered and transformed sentient beings. Within the first [section], there are three parts.
The passage from "First, the Buddhas... up to "...transforming sentient beings" cites the fundamental correct practice.

It establishes the great vow to deliver all realms of sentient beings without exception, extending to the end of the future, regardless of the number of kalpas. Next, the passage from "Next, establishing the great vow... up to "...the end of the future" [continues this].
This cites the fundamental great vow.
Within it, first is the vast mind,
followed by the long-term mind.

Because one takes all sentient beings as being like one’s own body, yet does not grasp at the mark of a sentient being—what is the meaning of this? It means that one knows, according to reality, that all sentient beings and one’s own body are equal in *tathatā* (suchness) and without distinction. To "take all" up to "equality in *tathatā*" [is as follows].
This refers to the great skillful means of compassion and wisdom;
it is also the non-perverted mind that regards others' possessions as one's own.
This reveals the profundity of compassion.
It may also explain the reason for attaining long duration as mentioned previously. Not grasping at the characteristics of objects reveals the profundity of wisdom.
By what meaning is this so?
The preceding inquiry seeks the reason for the profound depth of compassion and wisdom.
This means that by knowing [reality] as it truly is, one answers based on the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) to manifest that profundity. "Because there is such...
and so forth clarifies the citation of the cause to manifest the fruit.
Within this, there are also three [points].
Because there is such great wisdom of skillful means—this first restates the preceding cause.
"Eliminating ignorance and seeing the fundamental dharmakāya"—second, regarding the elimination of ignorance and the vision of the dharmakāya:
This is the fruit of self-benefit. Third, from "spontaneously" (*svayam*) onwards, the characteristics of its activity are correctly revealed;
this is the fruit of benefiting others.
Within this, there are three phrases.

Spontaneously there exists the inconceivable activity of various functions, which is equal to True Suchness (tathatā) and pervades all places; yet, furthermore, no characteristic of function can be apprehended. Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are solely the body of the Dharma-body and the characteristic of wisdom, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which possesses no realm of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Being free from deliberate effort, they are spoken of as "function" only because sentient beings obtain benefit through seeing and hearing them. This first clarifies that the profundity of function does not depend upon intentional mental application.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Just as the mani-jewel and the celestial drum accomplish their own functions without thought," and secondly,
"it is equal to True Suchness (tathatā) and pervades all places."
The manifestation of its function is vast,
because it accords with principle. Third,
the subsequent section clarifies that while the function is active, it is eternally quiescent.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason within this?
it is a challenge stating:
"The Buddha is endowed with the three bodies (trikāya)."
Why, then, is it said that there is no aspect of utility?
The commentary explains: "If one were to discard the responsive resonance between the stimulus and its response..."
The Tathāgata is solely the wondrous principle of fundamental wisdom;
there are no further marks of transformation, worldly convention, birth, or extinction.
He merely gives rise to functional manifestations in accordance with conditions.
Functioning is itself non-functioning,
just as waves are themselves water;
therefore, functioning is eternally quiescent.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"This body of mine is itself the Dharma-body. The *She-lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states:
Only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain alone;
this is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Therefore, it is said: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, even transcend all purposeful activity."
Although the wondrous wisdom of ultimate truth is fundamentally and eternally serene,
its utility for benefiting beings according to their capacities is boundless;
it is the constant functioning within stillness.
Therefore, it is said: "It merely follows sentient beings," and so forth, up to "for the sake of its distinct functions. Within the explanation of the functions, there are two parts:
first the heading, then the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are likewise two parts.
The first part correctly reveals the characteristics of its function;
the latter consists of questions and answers that resolve doubts.
Within the former, there are also two sections.
It continuously manifests its function.
Second, the double restatement and analysis.
Within the former, there are two parts.
First, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is explained; subsequently, the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is explained.

This [response body] has two aspects. What are these two? First, that which is seen by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, based on the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna* (consciousness of discriminating phenomena), is called the *nirmāṇakāya*. This is because they do not know that it is manifested by the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses); they see it as coming from outside, grasp at its material dimensions, and are unable to fully comprehend it. Regarding the phrase "based on the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna*" mentioned above: [End of excerpt]
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not yet understand that there is only consciousness (vijñaptimātra);
they reckon that external objects exist.
This is precisely the meaning of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the discerning consciousness of phenomena).
Now, seeing the Buddha-body, one also regards it as being outside the mind;
this is because it accords with the discriminative calculation of the *vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects), and thus it is said that one sees by relying on the discriminative *vastu-vijñāna*.
Furthermore, although such a person may be aware of the six consciousnesses, [they do not realize the nature of the eighth consciousness].
Because they do not perceive those seventh and eighth consciousnesses,
they rely solely on the *savisaya-vijnana* (consciousness of objects).
Based on this coarse consciousness, they discriminate the body of the Buddha.
One perceives only the coarse marks of the manifested transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and does not perceive the subtle marks of the recompense body (saṃbhogakāya); therefore,
it is called the "response body" (nirmāṇakāya).
The phrase "because they do not know that the evolving consciousnesses are manifest, up to being unable to fully know them" explains the reason why their vision is coarse.
Because they are deluded regarding "mind-only," it is said that [objects] arise from the outside.
Failing to realize that form is itself mind, there are no boundaries;
therefore, it is said that one cannot fully know [reality] by grasping at the boundaries of form.
Question: For what reason is the Buddha-body nothing other than the consciousness of sentient beings?
Answer: The true mind of sentient beings is equal and non-dual with the essence of all Buddhas.
However, sentient beings are deluded regarding their own true principle and give rise to false thoughts.
At that time, True Suchness manifests only defiled characteristics and its function is not revealed.
Because that fundamental awakening internally perfumes the deluded mind, there arises a sense of weariness with and a longing for [the truth].
Because this weariness and longing exist, the true function immediately manifests; yet, because this weariness and longing are weak, [full realization does not yet occur].
When the application of signs is coarse,
the longing for renunciation gradually increases,
and the application itself also gradually becomes subtle.
In this manner, proceeding gradually until reaching the source of the mind,
ignorance is exhausted; consequently,
both aversion and seeking are entirely stilled.
Initial awakening is identical to the fundamental;
its function returns to its essence,
which is equal and perfectly equal.
They are non-dual and without distinction.
Before reaching the source of the mind and even when returning [to it], they continue to manifest within consciousness according to the sense faculties;
therefore, it is said that they "manifest within consciousness."
Question: If, according to this principle,
activity arises from the True [Nature],
why is it said that the evolving consciousnesses manifest?
Answer: The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are precisely the evolving aspect (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) within the ālayavijñāna.
Based upon this evolving aspect, the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) arises and manifests all objective realms.
This consciousness is the union of the true and the false.
If one follows along with the flow of birth and death,
there is then a false efficacy; though this falsity possesses efficacy, [it remains unreal].
Apart from the True, nothing can be established; if one turns back and flows out into the entanglements, the True possesses functional power.
Although the True has this power, [it remains unmanifest].
Since it is not manifest apart from delusion, its function is explained only within the context of the consciousnesses that arise through dependent origination and are in a state of conjunction.
Question: If this is the meaning according to this principle...
This is precisely the functioning of *tathatā* within the minds of sentient beings themselves.
Why, then, do you speak of it as the Buddha’s recompense-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) or transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*)?
Answer: The true mind of sentient beings is the very essence of all Buddhas; there is no further distinction between them.
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"If anyone wishes to seek to know all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
they should contemplate in this manner."
"The mind creates all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta* states:
"The Dharma-body is itself sentient beings."
Sentient beings are themselves the Dharmakāya;
the Dharmakāya and sentient beings are identical in meaning though different in name.
Since the retributive and transformational functions arise from the Dharma-body,
how could they not be the true mind of sentient beings?
If this is the meaning of the question:
The Buddha within the minds of sentient beings returns to teach and transform those very sentient beings.
Why, then, is it said that this is due to the power of the Buddha’s compassion and vows?
The answer is: this very true mind is itself the Buddha’s compassion and vows.
This refers to objectless great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the vow for the non-obstruction of one's own essence, which is precisely the great functioning of the arising of nature (*dharmatā*).
Question: Since sentient beings have possessed minds from beginningless time, [how can they be liberated?]
"Why do you not rise early to transform and employ [the mind] so as to extinguish ignorance?
He replied, "Because there has been no sense of weariness with or seeking after it.
He asked, "Since there has always fundamentally existed original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi),..."
"Why do you not cultivate [the mind] early on to give rise to weariness with and seeking for [liberation]?
The answer is: "The thickness or thinness of ignorance differs, and causes and conditions are mutually deficient and unequal."
This is as explained above.
Question: If the true mind is itself the Buddha, why does the subsequent text state that it arises from causes such as the various pāramitās?
Answer: This is explained according to the principle of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) responding to conditions;
however, when initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi) awakens to the source of the mind, it is equal and of one single limit.
What is the distinction? Thus far, this has been explained according to the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya).
If explained according to the Initial Teaching (ādikarmika-naya), however:
Taking the compassion and wisdom of all Buddhas as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) and the seeds of sentient beings' responsive resonance as the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya),
[the image] thus relies upon the fundamental essence of the Buddha.
Because it is an image transformed by one's own mind, it is said to "manifest within one's own consciousness.
The rest is as explained in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Regarding the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), there are three types.
First, the person is identified by reference to consciousness;
second, from "the body has immeasurable [qualities]" onwards, the characteristics of the retribution seen are clarified;
third, the name "retribution" is explained and manifested by showing that the result arises from causes.

Second, regarding that which relies upon the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*): it is said that what is perceived by the minds of Bodhisattvas from their initial generation of the resolve until they reach the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Within the preceding [section], "relying upon the karmic consciousness" means:
From the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, Bodhisattvas are able to understand that there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and no external objects.

Because they perceive the Buddha-body in accordance with the principle of the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālaya-vijñāna*), it is called the "retribution body" (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). Regarding the characteristics of the perceived retribution body, there are two [aspects].

First the primary [body], then the basis. The body possesses immeasurable colors; each color possesses immeasurable marks; each mark possesses immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); and the fruits upon which it rests are likewise adorned with immeasurable varieties. According to what is manifested, they are boundless and inexhaustible, free from the characteristic of limitation. As appropriate to each case, they are always able to sustain themselves without being destroyed or lost. Regarding the primary [body], because the body has no limits, it is said to have "immeasurable colors."
Based on the body there are marks;
these marks are also limitless.
Based on the marks there are secondary characteristics.
The excellence is likewise inexhaustible.
Nevertheless, these marks serve to manifest his virtue,
enabling people to revere that virtue and thereby bring to mind the Buddha.
He is fond of adorning his body so as to inspire love and desire for intimacy in others.
Regarding the "immeasurable varieties of adornment" mentioned among the secondary rewards (*pratyaya-vipāka*):
Because that which depends [upon it] is boundless,
the land upon which it depends is likewise boundless,
consisting of exquisite jewels such as *pāṇḍukambala* and others.
Because it constantly emits light that is unimpeded and exquisitely adorned,
it is called "various adornments.
As for the statement "according to what is manifested, up to the point of being free from the marks of limitation":
It differs from the previous manifestations in that their boundaries are not fixed;
because this bodhisattva knows that what has boundaries is itself without boundaries,
every single characteristic of form pervades the entire dharma-realm.
They are mutually integrated and unimpeded,
for their sovereign mastery is inconceivable.
Thus, according to what is appropriate, they neither destroy nor lose [the teachings].
Whatever is to be experienced according to one's karmic actions remains eternally present;
it is not subject to destruction by the three calamities or the like.

Such merits are accomplished through the perfuming of untainted practices such as the *pāramitās* and the inconceivable perfuming; because they are fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss, they are called the *saṃbhogakāya*. This concludes the section on the analysis of the causes.
Thus, these inconceivable matters concerning the unimpeded nature of both the primary and secondary retributions are accomplished through two causes:
the permeation of the profound practice of the ten perfections and the inconceivable permeation of original enlightenment.
Because its marks of bliss are perfectly complete, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).
Thus it is said: "Such merits... are designated as the *saṃbhogakāya*. In the second section of the analysis, first the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body) and then the *saṃbhogakāya*.
One should distinguish here between the ordinary person and the Lesser Vehicle.

Furthermore, that which is perceived by ordinary persons is their coarse form; according to the six realms of existence, they each perceive it differently as various distinct types, and because it does not possess the characteristic of experiencing bliss, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). This is like the habitual perceptions of those in the three evil paths.
They see the Buddha with a body three feet tall, like the leg of a black elephant;
or, like Trapusa and others,
they see the Buddha from the perspective of the realms of humans and devas.
For tree spirits, celestial beings, and others,
it is according to this principle that sentient beings of the six realms each perceive the Buddha differently.
Because all these are not supramundane characteristics, they are not bliss. For instance,
those such as the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive the Buddha as supramundane,
[seeing him] as the physical body of noble beings such as Arhats.

Therefore it is said: "What is seen by ordinary beings, up to the response body (nirmāṇakāya). Within the section on the reward body (saṃbhogakāya), there is a distinction between the comparative and the realized;
herein there are two parts.
First, the vision of those prior to the stages (bhūmi) is clarified.

The following clarifies what is seen on the stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, regarding what is seen by bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds (*prathamacittotpādika*) and so forth: because they have deep faith in the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, they see it only partially. They perceive those matters of the adornment of forms and characteristics as being without coming or going, free from spatial limits, and manifesting solely in dependence upon the mind; yet they do not depart from *tathatā*. Nevertheless, these bodhisattvas still engage in conceptual discrimination because they have not yet entered the state of the *dharmakāya*. Once they attain the pure mind, what they see becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior until the end of the bodhisattva stages, where their vision reaches its ultimate consummation. If one is separated from the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), there is no aspect of seeing, for within the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas, there is no mutual seeing of each other through the characteristics of form or the distinctions of "this" and "that. Regarding the previous section, it says that through deep faith in the *tathatā* dharma, one sees it only partially.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of understanding (daśa-adhimukti) perceive the principle of *tathatā* by relying on the gate of inferential contemplation (*anumāna-dvāra*).
Because this is a semblance awakening (*pratirūpa-bodha*), it is called "partial" (*pradeśika*);
because it differs from the preceding ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), it is further described as "profound" (*gambhīra*).
Because it is a true realization distinct from what follows, it is simply called "faith.

As for the statement that one "knows those color-forms" up to "being free from limitations," this is because seeing True Suchness (tathatā) is distinct from that of ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Therefore, it is known that the nature of phenomena such as the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) is non-conceptual.
The statement that "they appear solely based on the mind and do not depart from *tathatā*" explains the reason for this non-conceptuality.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that "on the stages (bhūmi), one sees the reward body (saṃbhogakāya)," that is spoken from the perspective of the stage where realization is fully accomplished through its corresponding signs.
As for the present case, it refers to bodhisattvas prior to these stages who see [the reward body] only partially.
Because one knows that the objective realm of form is merely the manifesting consciousness, which is not separate from True Suchness (tathatā), and thus has no boundaries;
one thereby attains a partial vision.
Since it is not a complete vision,
there is no contradiction; however,
because it differs from the ordinary, limited mind that perceives external objects, one should see it as a manifestation (nirmāṇa).
Therefore, by summarizing the teaching of "mind-only," one gains a somewhat clear and distinct vision.
As for the statement that "this bodhisattva still engages in conceptual discrimination" and so forth,
it serves to distinguish this stage from those on the higher grounds (*bhūmi*).
The phrase "if one attains a pure mind" and below clarifies that the functional characteristics perceived on the stages (bhūmi) surpass those prior to the stages; therefore,
it is said to be "increasingly superior."
Gradually becoming subtle and refined,
until after the vajra-stage,
all karmic characteristics are completely exhausted.
Function returns to its essence;
therefore, it is said that one sees it to the ultimate limit,
for one has exhausted its source.
If one were apart from the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), there would be no aspect of seeing;

this is because it is only by depending upon the karmic consciousness that the aspect of transformation (*vivartalakṣaṇa*) and the aspect of manifestation (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*) exist. This is because even the Buddhas see one another.
If one is free from the ignorance of the karmic consciousness and so forth, there is only True Suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, the Buddha has no such dualistic views of "this" and "that. [Section Two: Dispelling Doubts, which consists of two parts.]
First the question, then the answer.
The question asks: "If the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is devoid of material form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), how can it manifest material forms? The answer also consists of two parts;
first, the explanation of how the Dharma-body is able to manifest.
Next, the colors manifested by the [receptive] consciousnesses are explained.
This section also has two parts;
first, the general [explanation].
Regarding the subsequent section on the "distinction of the lower," the answer states:

It is because this very *dharmakāya* is the substance of form (*rūpa*) that it can manifest as form. That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind are non-dual; since the nature of form is itself wisdom (*jñāna*), the substance of form is formless and is called the "wisdom-body" (*jñānakāya*). Since the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*), which pervades all places. Regarding the phrase "from the beginning, form and mind are non-dual": [it means that] they have never been separate.
This means that the manifested colors of retribution and transformation are not different from the true mind of the Dharma-body;
they are like waves and water, which are fundamentally non-dual.
As for the statement that "the nature of form is itself wisdom," and so forth:
Clarifying that form is mind reveals the non-duality before one; because form is mind,
the characteristics of form are thereby completely exhausted.
Therefore, regarding its fundamental nature, it is simply called the "Wisdom Body" (*jñānakāya*).
"Wisdom" refers to the mind of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

As for the statement that the Dharma-body pervades all places because the nature of wisdom is identical to form: [it means that because the essence of wisdom is itself material form, the Dharma-body is omnipresent].
Illuminating the mind as form reveals the non-duality mentioned previously;
it is like water pervading throughout the waves.

The forms that appear have no boundaries, yet they can manifest according to the mind the infinite worlds of the ten directions, the infinite reward bodies of bodhisattvas, and the infinite adornments, each distinct from the other. Though these are all without boundaries, they do not obstruct one another. This cannot be known through the discrimination of consciousness, for it is the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Within these manifested forms:
Because that true mind is unimpeded and all-pervasive,
the forms manifested by it are likewise perfectly interfused, sovereign, and unobstructed;
hence it is said that the manifested forms do not obstruct one another.
The immeasurable bodhisattvas therein are also the functioning of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*);
they may also be the conditions and opportunities that elicit the great activity of the reward body.
This is because they are all able to respond instantaneously;
for each and every faculty pervades the entire dharma-realm,
yet they do not obstruct one another.
The functioning of this True Suchness cannot be known by deluded consciousness;
therefore, it is said that it is not within the scope of mental consciousness discrimination, and so forth, up to its "functioning" (yòng).
The above concludes the two layers of meaning regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*yi*) within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing.
First, the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) is explained;
next, the gate of arising and ceasing is explained.
Altogether, this constitutes the first major section: the detailed explanation of the two gates.

The explanation of the meaning of non-identity is concluded. From here below is the second section, which correlates two gates to demonstrate their mutual inclusion and the reality of phenomena, thereby revealing the meaning of non-difference.
This section contains three parts.
First, the heading;
second, the explanation;
finally, the concluding summary.

Furthermore, it demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) directly from the gate of Arising and Ceasing (utpāda-nirodha). This refers to the thorough investigation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), wherein both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—as well as the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*)—are ultimately found to be without conceptualization (*animitta*). Since the mind has no form or characteristics, even if one searches throughout the ten directions, it can never be apprehended. Regarding the statement in the heading, "thoroughly investigating the five aggregates, form and mind": *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)*
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is form;
the other four are mind.
In the commentary, one first contemplates the phenomena of form.
Regarding the statement that the six sense objects are without thought:
objects arise from the mind and ultimately lack any inherent substance.
Apart from the mind, there are no characteristics that can be conceived.
When it is said that because the mind has no form, it cannot be found through seeking,
this means not only that there are no separate objects such as the six sense-fields (ṣaḍviṣaya) outside the mind.
Even when seeking the form and substance of color and so forth within the mind, they cannot be found.
In the former case, the object of perception (*ālambana*) is without marks;
in this case, the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*) does not arise. Below this follows the method for contemplating the mind.
First the analogy, then the application.

Just as a person, due to delusion, might take the east for the west while the direction itself does not actually change, so too it is with sentient beings: due to the delusion of ignorance, they take the mind to be thought, though the mind is in reality unmoving. Regarding the statement in the application that "the mind is in reality unmoving": [it means that the nature of the mind is fundamentally quiescent].
When one investigates the movement of thought,
it abides nowhere within that which has already ceased or that which has not yet arisen.
Because there is no place of abiding, there is no arising.
Therefore, one knows that the nature of the mind is truly unmoving.

If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one immediately attains compliance with and entry into the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā). The phrase "If one can" and those following it constitute the conclusion.
"Attaining immediate compliance" refers to the contemplation of skillful means.
"Entering the gateway of True Suchness" refers to...
